fields.title: Polka: the report that crashes stores
fields.summary: On Mondays, checkout takes 12 seconds instead of 400 ms. Decide how to separate reports and orders.
fields.decisionPrompt: How do we separate reports and orders?
fields.brief/role: You are the Polka product manager.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional local grocery delivery service. 900 partner stores.
fields.brief/context: Partners were given a personal dashboard with a sales report, and it's a success: 780 out of 900 stores log in weekly, and reporting has become the main argument in negotiations for connecting new ones. But on Mondays from 9 to 11, the buyer app lags: checkout takes up to 12 seconds instead of 400 ms, and conversion in this window is 23% lower.
fields.brief/objective: Remove report competition with order checkout without losing the argument in negotiations with chains.
fields.brief/constraints: Three large chains in the connection process, reporting named as a decisive factor. Conversion losses are about 340 thousand rubles a month.
fields.brief/task: Decide how to separate reports and orders and justify the cost of the decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Slow doesn't happen because the query is bad
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When two different types of load live in the same database, they compete for resources, and the one that suffers isn't necessarily the one at fault. Speeding up the query helps least here, and indexes can worsen what matters most: writing. Loads are separated into different places, and the choice between a temporary measure and an architectural solution is counted in money — how much a month of waiting costs versus a month of expense.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
"The report reads the same database as orders.

It gathers data across all store items for a period — this is a heavy query without an index, about 40 seconds.

On Mondays, hundreds run them simultaneously. The database is busy with them, and checkout transactions queue up waiting for locks.

It's not the query itself, but that report read load and order write load compete for a single resource."
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Report peak: Monday 9:00–11:00, up to 400 simultaneously.

Order peak: weekdays 18:00–21:00 and weekends.

Peak intersection: only Monday morning.

Checkout: 400 ms normally, up to 12 seconds in the intersection window.

Conversion on Monday morning is 23% lower.

780 out of 900 stores open the report weekly.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Conversion losses — about 340 thousand rubles a month.

Read-only database replica: three weeks of work, 60 thousand rubles a month.

Dedicated analytical storage: six weeks of work, 180 thousand rubles a month.

Indexes for report queries: a week and a half, no additional subscription fee.

Time restriction on reports: a week of work, no expenses.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Three large chains in the process of connecting; reporting named among decisive factors.

Two active partners request exports more often than once a day.

Stores look at the report on Mondays because Monday is procurement planning day.

No complaints about the speed of the report itself (40 seconds) have been received from partners yet.
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Three weeks, 60k per month. Reports read a copy updated with a delay of seconds.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
In three weeks, orders stop competing with reports: the customer journey returns to 400 ms on Monday mornings too.
Data delay in seconds for a period report is negligible — the partner is looking at yesterday's sales.
The heavy query remains heavy: the report still opens in 40 seconds, it just doesn't bother anyone now. There are no complaints about this, so the price is tolerable.
60k a month against 340k in losses — the expense pays off in the very first month.
This does not provide a foundation for future analytics: the request of two partners for frequent exports is not closed by this solution.
Trade-off: removed competition without solving the core task, and this is the right order — but the next step should be planned now, not when it hurts again.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Six weeks, 180k per month. Data is loaded hourly, structure tailored for reports.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Solves the task substantively: the report opens in a second instead of forty, load is separated architecturally.
This is the foundation for future analytics and what partners are asking for — but not in its current form: hourly data loading does not close two partners' request for frequent exports.
Six weeks of waiting cost about 500 thousand in lost conversion — more than the annual expense for a replica.
If choosing this without an interim step, you must explain why three weeks of work on a replica do not pay off half a million.
Trade-off: the right goal, paid for with six weeks of bleeding.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: One week. Dashboard unavailable from 18:00 to 21:00 and on Mondays until 12:00.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Cheap and fast: the bleeding stops in a week.
But exactly that window when it is most convenient for partners is closed: Monday is procurement planning day, and the report is needed precisely then.
To three connecting chains, this is a bad signal: reporting is named a decisive factor, yet we restrict it.
The root cause is not eliminated: growth in the number of stores will bring the problem back, just in a different window.
Trade-off: as a sole solution, it shifts pain from buyer to partner; as an immediate measure tied with B or C, it's reasonable.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Indexes for report queries on the main database
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: A week and a half. Query speeds up to about 4 seconds.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
Fast and without subscription fees, the report really speeds up tenfold.
But every index slows down writes — and writing is precisely the bottleneck in the evening order peak, which is unrelated to reports.
That means the auxiliary scenario is accelerated at the cost of the main one, and degradation will hit where it isn't expected.
Resource competition is not eliminated: four seconds on four hundred simultaneous reports will still occupy the database.
Trade-off: the cheapest option turns out to be the most dangerous, and rejecting it with this explanation is a strong move.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not distinguish transactional and analytical load
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Does not account for data delay as a product property
